title: Cervical spinal cord injury and neurogenic shock

header.contentArea: Trauma: spinal cord injury (clinical scenario with examiner-supplied findings)

brief.role: Core surgical trainee on the trauma team
brief.scenario: Mr Lewis Drummond, 34, came off his motorcycle at speed. He arrives with a collar, head blocks and scoop stretcher. He is alert. BP 85/50 mmHg, heart rate 52, warm dry feet. He cannot move his legs.
brief.task: Answer the examiner's questions on his assessment and management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Protect the spine, find the bleeding first, then call it neurogenic shock and treat it.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Blaming the hypotension on the cord before looking for haemorrhage.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Catastrophic haemorrhage, then airway with manual in-line stabilisation."

grid.label: Primary survey with spinal protection
grid.fail: Removes the collar to examine the neck, or ignores breathing.
grid.pass: <C>ABCDE with manual in-line stabilisation during any airway intervention; log roll; watches for respiratory failure.
grid.high: Explains the diaphragm is C3 to C5, so a cervical cord injury can progress to ventilatory failure: early anaesthetic and critical care input.

grid.label: Excludes haemorrhage
grid.fail: Attributes the hypotension to the cord injury without looking for bleeding.
grid.pass: Treats hypotension as haemorrhage until excluded: chest, abdomen, pelvis, long bones, external; FAST and trauma CT.
grid.high: Notes that cord injury can mask abdominal pain and tachycardia, so bleeding may be clinically silent.

grid.label: Recognises neurogenic shock
grid.fail: Cannot explain why he is bradycardic and warm.
grid.pass: Neurogenic shock: loss of sympathetic outflow below a lesion above T6, giving vasodilatation, hypotension and bradycardia with warm peripheries.
grid.high: Sympathetic outflow is T1 to L2 and cardiac accelerator fibres T1 to T4, so vagal tone is unopposed.

grid.label: Separates spinal shock
grid.fail: Uses spinal shock and neurogenic shock interchangeably.
grid.pass: Spinal shock is neurological: temporary flaccid paralysis, areflexia and sensory loss below the lesion, lasting hours to weeks.
grid.high: Completeness cannot be judged until spinal shock resolves; return of the bulbocavernosus reflex is classically used as its end.

grid.label: Blood pressure and heart rate
grid.fail: Gives repeated large fluid boluses, or ignores the bradycardia.
grid.pass: Cautious fluid, then a vasopressor with an arterial line in critical care; treats bradycardia with adverse signs.
grid.high: Targets MAP at least 75 to 80 mmHg, not pushed beyond 90 to 95, for 3 to 7 days.

grid.label: Imaging and neurology
grid.fail: Relies on plain films, or stops at a normal CT despite a deficit.
grid.pass: CT first; MRI after CT for any deficit that could be cord injury, even if CT is normal. ISNCSCI chart within 2 hours.
grid.high: Requests whole-spine MRI once safe, and states the neurological level from the chart: C5 here.

grid.label: Specialist care
grid.fail: Gives methylprednisolone, or does not contact the spinal team.
grid.pass: Immediate spinal surgeon referral; linked spinal cord injury centre. No methylprednisolone, nimodipine or naloxone for neuroprotection.
grid.high: Early decompression within 24 hours where feasible; catheter, pressure care and nasogastric tube for ileus.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd take the collar off to examine his neck properly.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It's the spinal injury. That explains it.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'm not sure. Maybe he's fit.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The same as neurogenic shock: low blood pressure after a spinal injury.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How would you treat the blood pressure?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Two litres of fluid, then more if needed.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: <C>ABCDE, keeping manual in-line stabilisation during any airway intervention, and log rolling. I'd watch his breathing closely.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Haemorrhage until proven otherwise. I'd look in the chest, abdomen, pelvis, long bones and externally, with a FAST scan and trauma CT.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: No bleeding is found. Heart rate 52, feet warm.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That's neurogenic shock. A lesion above T6 cuts sympathetic outflow, so he vasodilates and becomes bradycardic.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Spinal shock is neurological: temporary flaccid paralysis, areflexia and sensory loss below the lesion, lasting hours to weeks.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How would you manage his circulation?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Cautious fluid, then a vasopressor with an arterial line in critical care. If bradycardia has adverse signs, atropine 500 micrograms, repeated up to 3 mg.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: CT first, then MRI because he has a deficit, even if CT is normal. And a full ISNCSCI chart within 2 hours.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The spinal surgeon on call now, and the linked spinal cord injury centre. No steroids, nimodipine or naloxone.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The diaphragm is C3 to C5 and he's lost his intercostals, so he can tire and fail. I'd involve anaesthetics and critical care early.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: His abdomen is soft and non-tender.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That doesn't reassure me. With a cord injury he may feel no pain and can't mount a tachycardia, so I'd still image.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Sympathetic outflow is T1 to L2 and the cardiac accelerator fibres are T1 to T4. Lose them and vagal tone is unopposed.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I can't say until spinal shock resolves. Return of the bulbocavernosus reflex is classically taken as its end.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What blood pressure are you aiming for?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Current guidance suggests a MAP of at least 75 to 80, not pushed beyond 90 to 95, for 3 to 7 days. If bradycardia resists atropine, aminophylline is an option in cord injury.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Then whole-spine MRI once safe. His chart puts the level at C5: elbow flexion but no wrist extension. I'd also ask for CT angiography for vertebral artery injury.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Decompression within 24 hours where feasible. Meanwhile a catheter, pressure care and a nasogastric tube for ileus.

failures.move: Attributing hypotension to neurogenic shock without looking for bleeding.
failures.consequence: Occult haemorrhage from the abdomen or pelvis goes untreated in a patient who cannot feel it.

failures.move: Repeated large fluid boluses for neurogenic hypotension.
failures.consequence: Fluid overload and pulmonary oedema without correcting the vasodilatation.
NICE advises against it; it adds risk without proven neurological benefit.

failures.move: Removing spinal protection to examine the neck.
failures.consequence: Risks worsening an unstable cervical injury.

recovery.line: Neurogenic shock is the circulation; spinal shock is the neurology.
Bleeding first; only then neurogenic shock.

knowledge.fact: Neurogenic shock: hypotension, bradycardia and vasodilatation with lesions above T6.
Spinal shock: temporary flaccid areflexia and sensory loss below the lesion.
MRI after CT for any deficit that could be cord injury; no methylprednisolone, nimodipine or naloxone.
ISNCSCI chart within 2 hours of admission; whole-spine MRI once safe.
Suggested MAP at least 75–80 mmHg, not above 90–95 mmHg, for 3–7 days.
Bradycardia with adverse signs: atropine 500 micrograms, repeat to 3 mg; consider aminophylline in cord injury.
Cervical fracture or subluxation: CT angiography to exclude blunt cerebrovascular injury.

recall.think: Hidden haemorrhage, ventilatory failure, cord ischaemia.
recall.say: "Hypotension is bleeding until excluded; then neurogenic shock."
recall.trap: Warm feet and a slow pulse do not exclude bleeding.
recall.finish: Early decompression and transfer to a spinal cord injury centre.

sources.name: NICE NG41: Spinal injury: assessment and initial management
sources.supports: <C>ABCDE with manual in-line spinal immobilisation during airway intervention (1.1.1–1.1.2); CT in adults then MRI after CT for any neurological abnormality attributable to cord injury (1.5.6–1.5.7); immediate contact by the trauma team leader with the on-call specialist neurosurgical or spinal surgeon (1.6.2); do not use methylprednisolone, nimodipine or naloxone (1.7.3)

partner.opening: He has just arrived. Talk me through your initial approach.

reveals.finding: RR 24, shallow; abdominal breathing; SpO2 95% on oxygen.
Chest clear on X-ray; FAST negative; pelvis stable on X-ray; no long bone or external bleeding.
Elbow flexion present; no wrist extension or hand function; no leg movement; sensation preserved over the lateral upper arm, absent from C6 downwards; priapism; flaccid, areflexic limbs.

push.question: Why is he hypotensive?
push.expect: Haemorrhage until excluded, then neurogenic shock.

push.question: Why is he bradycardic with warm feet?
push.expect: Loss of sympathetic tone above T6; unopposed vagal tone.

push.question: What is spinal shock?
push.expect: Temporary neurological loss below the lesion; not a haemodynamic state.

push.question: How will you support his blood pressure?
push.expect: Cautious fluid, vasopressor, arterial line, critical care.

curveballs.prompt: During suctioning his heart rate falls to 35 and he becomes grey.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Stop the stimulus, atropine 500 micrograms, repeat to 3 mg; call for help; aminophylline or pacing if refractory.

curveballs.prompt: Weeks later his BP is 210/110 with a pounding headache.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Autonomic dysreflexia: sit him up, find the trigger below the lesion (often bladder or bowel), treat it.

curveballs.prompt: The FAST scan shows free fluid.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Haemorrhagic shock takes priority: blood products and haemorrhage control; neurogenic shock may coexist.
